opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, manufacturing defects are a really interesting stress test for auto-labeling, and honestly a humbling one. A few things make it hard.

First, the defects themselves are rare. On a production line, the overwhelming majority of what you see is a perfectly good part. So you have a massive class imbalance, and the thing you actually care about, the scratch or the hairline crack or the misaligned component, is a tiny sliver of the data. Auto-labeling approaches built on foundation models do well on common, visually salient categories, the "car," "person," "dog" kinds of things that show up all over internet-scale training data. A subtle surface anomaly on a machined part is nowhere near that distribution.

Second, the defects are often physically small and low-contrast. You might be looking for a few pixels of discoloration on a large, high-resolution image. Many zero-shot detectors and segmenters are biased toward objects at a certain scale with clear boundaries, so they either miss these regions entirely or produce boxes that are sloppy relative to how tight the region really needs to be.

Third, and I think this is underappreciated, the notion of what a defect even *is* is highly domain-specific and sometimes ambiguous. What counts as an acceptable cosmetic variation versus a reject is defined by the manufacturer's spec, and even experienced human inspectors disagree at the margins. So when you try to measure auto-labeling performance, your ground truth is itself noisier and more subjective than in a typical benchmark. You can't just say the model got 70% and call it a day; you have to ask whether the disagreement is the model being wrong or the label being fuzzy.

And then there's the cost asymmetry. In a lot of applications, a missed label is just a slightly worse training set. In manufacturing, a missed defect can mean a faulty part ships to a customer, and a false alarm can mean throwing away good product or stopping a line. So the evaluation can't just be an aggregate metric; you really care about the failure modes, and where the confidence thresholds should sit.

So for us, it was a domain that really exposed where auto-labeling works well, which is the common, well-represented cases, and where you still very much need humans in the loop, which is the rare, subtle, and spec-driven cases. It pushed us toward thinking about auto-labeling not as a replacement for annotation, but as a way to triage, getting the easy stuff done fast so human expertise goes where it actually matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so manufacturing defects are kind of a fascinating case, because on the surface it looks like one of the easier problems. You've got a fixed camera, controlled lighting, the same part coming down the line over and over. It feels like the dream setup for a vision model. But when you actually try to evaluate how well an auto-labeling system is doing, it falls apart for a few reasons.

The first is just the base rates. Defects are rare, right? That's the whole point of a good manufacturing process. So you might have a hundred thousand images and a few hundred actual defects. If an auto-labeler just says "no defect" on everything, it looks fantastic on accuracy, and it's completely useless. So you have to be really careful about what metric you're even looking at, and you need enough positive examples to say anything meaningful about recall, which is the number the customer actually cares about. Missing a defect is expensive. A false alarm is annoying, but a miss can mean a recall or a safety issue.

The second thing is that the defects themselves are often tiny and visually ambiguous. We're talking a scratch that's a few pixels wide, or a subtle discoloration, or a slight warp in a surface. And when I say ambiguous, I mean ambiguous to humans too. You can put the same image in front of three quality inspectors and get three different answers about whether that's a defect or just acceptable variation. So when you're assessing auto-labeling performance, the question becomes, performance against what? Your ground truth itself has noise in it. And if your reference labels are inconsistent, you genuinely can't tell whether the model is wrong or the human was.

And then there's a third piece, which is that the categories aren't stable. A manufacturer will say, we have twelve defect classes, and then you look at the data and realize class four and class seven are basically the same thing depending on who labeled it, and there's a thirteenth thing showing up that nobody has a name for yet, because the process changed last month. So the auto-labeler might be doing something reasonable, and it still looks bad because the taxonomy it was handed doesn't match reality.

So what we've found is that you can't just run a benchmark and get a number. You have to look at the disagreements. You have to go case by case, especially on the rare positives, and actually understand where the model and the annotators diverge and why. That's slow, and it's uncomfortable, because it often ends up being as much an assessment of the labeling process as of the model. But that's honestly where the signal is in this domain.

r001.rationale: The response describes rare defects and unstable defect categories, but does not compare the number of possible defect forms with the correct manufacturing outcomes.

r002.rationale: It mentions a new defect category appearing after a process change, but does not clearly state that the range of possible defect types is difficult to predict.

astra-6.text:
Manufacturing defects are difficult because the things you care about are often very rare. You might have lots of images of good parts, but only a handful of examples of a particular defect. And defects can be subtle—a small scratch or a slight change in texture—and whether something counts as a defect can depend on the specific manufacturing process and its tolerances.

That makes assessing auto-labeling tricky. If you measure performance across all the images, you can get a very high score simply by labeling everything as normal. What you really need to understand is whether you're finding those rare defects, and whether the labels are precise enough to be useful. With so few examples, it's hard to get a reliable estimate of that.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, manufacturing defects are difficult because the thing you’re looking for is often very rare. You might have thousands of examples of a good part and just a handful of defective ones. And those defects can vary quite a bit—a scratch, a crack, a small change in texture—so it’s hard to know whether those few examples really capture what you’ll encounter.

That also makes evaluating auto-labeling tricky. If you measure performance across all the images, you can get a very high score simply by calling almost everything normal. But the question that matters is whether you’re finding the defects, including the unusual ones, and whether you’re locating them precisely enough to be useful. With so few examples, it’s difficult to make a confident assessment of that.
